title: Frank Worrell Unites the West Indies
text:
For decades the West Indies cricket team had been led by white captains, even though most of its players were Black. The team was also split by rivalries among the islands it drew on, Jamaica, Barbados, Trinidad, Guyana and others, which sometimes made it play like a collection of individuals. In 1960, after a long public campaign, including writing by C. L. R. James, the Barbadian batsman Frank Worrell was appointed captain for a tour of Australia, the first Black cricketer to lead the West Indies for a full series.

Worrell was calm, dignified and fair, and he treated players from every island alike. He asked his team to play attacking, entertaining cricket and to behave as one side.

The first Test, at Brisbane in December 1960, ended in the first tie in the history of Test cricket, with the last Australian batsman run out on the penultimate ball of the final over. The series that followed was close and played in an exceptional spirit. Australia won it narrowly, two matches to one, but the West Indies had won the public. When they left, crowds estimated in the hundreds of thousands lined the streets of Melbourne to see them off. A trophy named after Worrell has been contested by the two countries ever since.

Worrell went on to lead the West Indies to victory in England in 1963. He was knighted in 1964 and died of leukemia in 1967, aged 42.
lesson: A leader who treats everyone fairly can turn rival factions into one team. How a team plays together can matter as much as the result.
people: Frank Worrell, C. L. R. James, Richie Benaud, Wes Hall
source: Match records; C. L. R. James, Beyond a Boundary (1963)
